prompt: An organisation changes a deep reporting tree into a flat tree, keeping all the same people and one root. What happens to the number of reporting lines?

options.text: It increases because the root has more direct reports.
options.explanation: Other manager links disappear as root links are added.

options.text: It decreases because there are fewer levels.
options.explanation: Depth and edge count are different properties.

options.text: It stays the same: every non-root person still has one manager link.
options.explanation: Each such person accounts for exactly one edge.

options.text: It depends on how many leaves the new tree has.
options.explanation: Every tree on the same vertices has the same edge count.

workedExample: Count lines by the person reporting, rather than by tree shape. Every person except the root contributes exactly one manager link. Changing who manages whom changes paths and depths but not the number of contributors, provided the structure remains a tree.

prompt: Kruskal’s algorithm accepts an edge only when its endpoints lie in different components. What does each accepted edge do?

options.explanation: Joining two components merges them rather than creating another.

options.text: It always completes a spanning tree.
It creates one cycle inside a component.
options.explanation: That is exactly the edge Kruskal rejects.

options.text: It reduces the component count by one and preserves acyclicity.
options.explanation: There was no existing path between its endpoints, so joining them cannot close a cycle.

workedExample: Two separate trees become one tree after adding a connecting edge. All other components remain unchanged. Repeating this explains the forest edge-count relationship. A spanning tree is possible only if the original graph provides enough connections between all components.
